question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Robert Clive — Key battles and their locations]
options: Battle of Plassey (1757) — Fought near the village of Palashi on the banks of the Bhagirathi (Hooghly) river in Bengal
Siege of Arcot (1751) — Robert Clive captured and held Arcot (capital of the Carnatic) with a small force for 50 days
Battle of Buxar (1764) — Fought at Buxar on the banks of the Ganga; Clive personally commanded the EIC forces to victory
Battle of Plassey (1757) — Mir Jafar was the betraying general whose defection ensured the British victory over Siraj-ud-Daulah
wrong_fact: Robert Clive did NOT personally command British forces at the Battle of Buxar (1764). The Battle of Buxar was commanded by Major Hector Munro. Clive was in England during the battle and returned to India only in 1765 as Governor after the victory.
explanation: The Battle of Buxar (22 October 1764) was fought by British forces under Major Hector Munro against the combined forces of Mir Qasim (Nawab of Bengal), Shuja-ud-Daula (Nawab of Awadh), and the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II. Robert Clive had no role in this battle — he returned to India in 1765 (after the battle) and signed the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) with Shah Alam II, which gave the British the Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Robert Clive — Treaties, regions, and their significance]
options: Treaty of Allahabad (1765) — Granted Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa to the British East India Company
Dual Government (1765–72) — Clive's system where EIC held Diwani rights and Nawab retained Nizamat (police/judicial) power
Murshidabad — Capital of Bengal under Siraj-ud-Daulah where the Black Hole incident occurred before Plassey
Fort St. George (Madras) — Clive first entered EIC service here as a clerk before his military career in the Carnatic
wrong_fact: The 'Black Hole of Calcutta' incident did NOT occur at Murshidabad. It occurred at Fort William in Calcutta (Kolkata) on the night of 20 June 1756, when Siraj-ud-Daulah's forces captured Fort William and allegedly imprisoned British prisoners in a small room.
explanation: The Black Hole of Calcutta incident (June 1756) took place at Fort William, Calcutta, not at Murshidabad (which was the Nawab's capital). After capturing Calcutta, Siraj allegedly imprisoned over 100 British prisoners overnight in a small cell — many died. This event was the direct trigger for Clive's expedition from Madras to recapture Calcutta, culminating in the Battle of Plassey (1757). The Treaty of Allahabad (1765) and Dual Government system are correctly described.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Robert Clive — Governorships and administrative geography]
options: First Governorship of Bengal (1757–60) — Clive installed Mir Jafar as Nawab and received the Zamindari of 24 Parganas for the EIC
Second Governorship of Bengal (1765–67) — Clive enacted the Dual Government system and issued the Clive Fund (military reform)
Zamindari of 24 Parganas — Granted by Mir Jafar to the EIC in 1757, giving British effective control over the region south of Calcutta
Awadh (Oudh) — Clive permanently annexed Awadh as a British territory after the Battle of Buxar (1764) via the Treaty of Allahabad
wrong_fact: Awadh was NOT annexed by Clive after the Battle of Buxar. Via the Treaty of Allahabad (1765), Clive restored Awadh to Shuja-ud-Daula (in exchange for a large indemnity) and used it as a buffer state. Awadh was only formally annexed by the British in 1856 under Lord Dalhousie.
explanation: After the Battle of Buxar (1764), Clive signed two treaties at Allahabad (1765): one with Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II (granting EIC Diwani rights over Bengal, Bihar, Orissa) and another with Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh (restoring Awadh in exchange for a war indemnity and territorial cession of Kara and Allahabad). Awadh was kept as a buffer state — a deliberate strategic choice — and was not annexed until 1856. The 24 Parganas grant (1757) and Dual Government (1765) are correctly matched.
